content: The hemoglobin concentration among adolescent girls was of high quality. However, no evidence was provided regarding malaria-related morbidity. Adherence to the intervention may be a concern if it is perceived as non-essential. Barriers to adherence, such as the perception of necessity among beneficiaries, may need to be addressed through behavior-change communication strategies. Studies measuring compliance showed that 65% to 98% of the tablets were consumed, with no significant difference between the iron supplementation and control groups. The cost of implementing daily iron supplementation in this population is influenced more by operational challenges than the cost of the supplement itself. Distributing daily iron supplements, especially in settings where healthcare interventions do not specifically target menstruating women and adolescent girls, may present logistical challenges. Adequate resources and investments should be considered when designing programs to reach this population. Daily oral iron supplementation is a preventive strategy intended for population-level implementation. If a menstruating woman is diagnosed with anemia, national guidelines for anemia treatment should be followed. The prevalence of anemia should guide the dose, duration, and frequency of iron supplementation among menstruating women and adolescent girls. For anemia prevalence rates below 40%, alternative guidelines, such as intermittent iron supplementation regimens, may be considered. Daily iron supplementation should be evaluated in the context of other iron-containing interventions, such as fortified foods, multiple micronutrient powders, and lipid-based nutrient supplements. The choice of delivery platform should be context-specific, aiming to reach the most vulnerable populations and ensuring a continuous and timely supply of supplements. All women attempting to conceive and up to 12 weeks of gestation should take folic acid supplements. Daily oral iron and folic acid supplementation should be part of routine antenatal care, initiated as early as possible and continued throughout pregnancy. In areas with high anemia prevalence (40% or more) among pregnant women, supplementation should extend for three months postpartum. Iron supplementation is a standard intervention for addressing anemia but should ideally be part of a comprehensive, integrated program for anemia reduction and women’s health across the life course. Interventions to reduce iron deficiency or iron-deficiency anemia should include nutrition counseling to promote dietary diversity and food combinations that enhance iron absorption, malaria-control programs (e.g., intermittent preventive treatment during pregnancy and use of insecticide-treated bed nets), control of parasitic infections, and improved sanitation. Delayed umbilical cord clamping is effective in preventing iron deficiency in infants and young children. Other options include fortifying staple foods and providing micronutrient powders containing iron. The dissemination of these guidelines will occur through electronic media, including slide presentations, the WHO nutrition website, and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). The guidelines will also be shared through WHO’s network of international partners, including country and regional offices, ministries of health, collaborating centers, universities, and NGOs. Tailored derivative products, such as summaries and compilations of recommendations, will be developed to meet the needs of end-users. Implementation of these guidelines should be adapted to the context of each Member State. Public health programs providing iron supplements to menstruating women and adolescent girls should have clear objectives, considering available resources, existing policies, delivery platforms, communication channels, and stakeholders. Iron supplementation should ideally be part of an integrated program addressing adolescent and reproductive health, including micronutrient deficiencies. Ongoing assessment of the accessibility and acceptability of the intervention can inform program design and development to improve adherence and evaluate the program’s impact. This is particularly relevant in settings where social norms and determinants may create unequal conditions and opportunities for different groups. For example, social perceptions related to ethnicity and race may influence how certain population groups access and use interventions. Supplementation programs for menstruating women and adolescent girls should be carefully designed based on locally available evidence and experience. This includes data on procurement, supply-chain issues, optimal distribution channels, behavior-change communication, and strategies to identify and reach the most vulnerable populations. Reaching hard-to-access groups is critical during implementation to address health inequities. Appropriate surveillance and monitoring systems are essential to evaluate the impact of the guidelines and their implementation, including funding adequacy and the effectiveness of supply chains and distribution channels. Monitoring differences in accessibility, availability, acceptability, and quality of interventions across groups contributes to better public health program design. The WHO Essential Medicines List (EML) includes medicines that address priority healthcare needs, selected based on disease prevalence, evidence of efficacy and safety, and cost-effectiveness. The EML serves as a reference for countries developing their national essential medicines lists. Quality criteria for vitamins and minerals in the EML align with FAO/WHO standards. WHO has developed a logic model for micronutrient interventions in public health, which Member States can adapt for designing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating nutrition actions. The WHO/CDC eCatalogue of indicators for micronutrient programs provides a user-friendly resource for monitoring and evaluation. The guideline development process followed WHO’s evidence-informed procedures, involving advisory groups such as the WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development, a guideline development group, and an external review group. The process included systematic reviews, evidence appraisal using the GRADE approach, and consultations with experts. Management of competing interests adhered to WHO’s strict guidelines. Participants acted in their individual capacity, and any conflicts of interest were disclosed and addressed appropriately.
